pass_a_gloss: [their words continue] … let us shut up in a tomb the immortal one, let us remove the wonder out of the way, from which such great terrors come to us. §19 But even having done these things, they profited nothing of their aim; and the thing attempted turns out for them into the opposite. And for this reason they said in the evening: 'How might it become morning?' Since again fearful were the wonders accomplished in the night of the resurrection, since they saw the tomb as a bridal chamber, the grave sealed and the dead man running out with life, the soldiers as dead [Matthew 28:4], the women carrying myrrh, angels guarding the linen cloths, another sitting on the stone as herald of the resurrection [Matthew 28:2], then they said: 'How might it become morning?' so that we may give silver coins to the soldiers, so that we may corrupt Pilate, so that we may steal the truth by deceit, so that we may put about the report 'that his disciples, coming by night, stole him while we were sleeping' [Matthew 28:12-14]. §20 These things the law, and Moses through it, and rather God in each of these, testifies against the unthankful people; and Stephen the theologian, convicting it, is named a blasphemer by them. And the high priest says: 'Are these things so?' [Acts 7:1]. For do you not know how they are? Did you not prepare the trick? Did you not hire the slanderers? Do not the witnesses of the deceit work for wages for you? 'But there is need,' he says, 'of lying and hypocrisy; and of deceit we have need for the snare put forward. Thus we sold Joseph [Genesis 37:28], we murdered Naboth [1 Kings 21:13], we crucified Christ.' §21 But Stephen, finding an opportunity of teaching, poured out many saving things into the ears of the people, and brought on as the conclusion of his oratory words fitting both for himself to speak, as a witness of truth, and for those men to hear, as men set on fighting God and sick with contradiction of the Spirit: 'Hard of heart and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always fall against the Holy Spirit; as your fathers, so also you' [Acts 7:51]. §22 And how at the beginning do you say: 'Men, brothers and fathers, hear me' [Acts 7:2]? 'Those words,' he says, 'are of the nobility of Abraham, but these of their wickedness. Those of the good root, these of the wicked branches. Those show what is distinguished in the flock, these the disorder, the hardness, the unbridled state of the many.' Toward that opening Isaiah urged him: 'Say, our brothers, to those who hate us and loathe us, so that the name of the Lord may be glorified' [Isaiah 66:5]. But toward this end they themselves, even against his intention, force the speech: 'I called them brothers, I addressed them as fathers, lest anyone suppose that I accuse them as enemies, that I refute them as foes. But the same men I addressed as hard of heart and uncircumcised, since one must honour truth above kinship and spare neither friends nor brothers nor fathers nor other relatives when they break the law.' §23 The children of the Jews, however, did not endure these words, but gnashed their teeth like wild beasts, hurrying to swallow down Stephen while he was still speaking. 'They gnashed their teeth' [Acts 7:54]. For about them it had been said: 'Sons of men, their teeth weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword' [Psalm 56:5 LXX]. But Stephen held his eyes not toward them but toward God, and letting go of the earth he pressed on into the courts of the heavens, and with a bright voice he proclaimed: 'Behold, I see the heavens opened' [Acts 7:56]. That is: the gain is common, the road ready for all, the gate has been opened to those wishing to enter. Let the brave man contend strenuously; let the genuine soldier now use his weapons, now display the greatness of his strength. For the president of the games looks on; he stands by, distributing the crowns and the prizes. §24 'Behold, I see the heavens opened.' And who it was that opened, he did not let the one who wishes to know be ignorant. And for this reason he cried out: 'And the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God' [Acts 7:56], speaking of God the Word made flesh. For since the Son of God has become Son of Man, since the one from the Father has himself, from a virgin, stood as boundary for the earth and the heavens, the middle wall of the enmity has been removed [Ephesians 2:14], the fence is out of the way, the things of citizenship are common to the angels and to men, if men are willing. It is possible for those who are on earth to serve as soldiers in heaven, to be below in the flesh, to be present above in the spirit, to be with the clay by the clay, but with God by the mind. §25 These things, then, Stephen spoke as theology; but disorderly shouts followed the theology in order, and shouts succeeded the shouts; and slings of stones followed the teachings of the holy laws [the verb ἐπηκολούθουν opens the next section].
pass_b_english: …shut up the Immortal in a tomb, and rid ourselves of the wonder from which such great terrors come upon us?”

But even when they had done these things, they gained nothing of their aim; what they attempted turned out the opposite for them. And this is why in the evening they said, “When will it be morning?” For again the wonders worked in the night of the resurrection were fearful: they saw the tomb as a bridal chamber, the grave sealed and the dead man running out alive, the soldiers like dead men (Matthew 28:4), the women bearing myrrh, angels guarding the linen cloths, and another sitting on the stone as herald of the resurrection (Matthew 28:2). Then they said: “When will it be morning, so that we may give silver to the soldiers, so that we may corrupt Pilate, so that we may steal the truth by deceit, so that we may spread the report ‘that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep’?” (Matthew 28:12-14).

This is the testimony the law bears, and Moses through it, or rather God in each of them, against the thankless people; and Stephen the theologian, for convicting that people, is called a blasphemer by them. And the high priest says: “Are these things so?” (Acts 7:1). Do you not know how they are? Did you not contrive the plot? Did you not hire the slanderers? Are not the witnesses of the deceit in your pay? “But there is need,” he says, “of falsehood and pretense, and we need deceit for the trap we have laid. So we sold Joseph (Genesis 37:28), so we murdered Naboth (1 Kings 21:13), so we crucified Christ.”

But Stephen, having found an occasion for teaching, poured many saving words into the people’s ears, and as the conclusion of his speech he brought in words fit for him to say, as a witness of the truth, and for them to hear, as men bent on fighting against God and sick with opposition to the Spirit: “Hard-hearted and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you” (Acts 7:51).

And how is it that at the beginning you say, “Men, brothers and fathers, hear me” (Acts 7:2)? “Those words,” he says, “belong to the nobility of Abraham, these to the wickedness of these men. Those belong to the good root, these to the bad branches. Those show what is distinguished in the flock, these the unruliness, the hardness, the unbridled temper of the many.” Isaiah urged him toward that opening: “Say ‘Our brothers’ to those who hate us and abhor us, so that the name of the Lord may be glorified” (Isaiah 66:5). But toward this ending they themselves forced his speech, even against his will: “I called them brothers, I addressed them as fathers, so that no one would think I was accusing them as enemies or refuting them as foes. But I called the same men hard-hearted and uncircumcised, since truth must be put before kinship, and one must not spare friends or brothers or fathers or any other relatives when they break the law.”

Yet the children of the Jews could not bear these words, but gnashed their teeth like wild beasts, eager to swallow Stephen up while he was still speaking. “They gnashed their teeth” (Acts 7:54). For of them it had been said: “Sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Psalm 57:4). But Stephen kept his eyes not on them but on God, and leaving the earth behind he hastened toward the courts of heaven, and with a ringing voice he proclaimed: “Look, I see the heavens opened” (Acts 7:56). That is: the gain is shared, the way is ready for all, the gate has been opened to those who wish to enter. Let the brave man contend with all his strength; let the true soldier now use his weapons, now show the greatness of his might. For the one who presides over the contest is watching; he stands ready, handing out the crowns and the prizes.

“Look, I see the heavens opened.” And he did not leave the one who wishes to know in ignorance of who opened them. For this reason he cried out: “and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:56), meaning God the Word made flesh. For since the Son of God has become Son of Man, since he who is from the Father has himself come from a virgin and stood as the common border of earth and the heavens, the dividing wall of enmity has been taken away (Ephesians 2:14), the barrier is out of the way, and citizenship is shared by angels and men, if men are willing. Those who are on earth may serve as soldiers in heaven, be below in the flesh and present above in the spirit, be with the clay by the clay, but with God by the mind.
Such, then, was the theology Stephen proclaimed; but disorderly shouts followed his orderly theology, and shout followed shout; and stones from slings followed the teachings of the holy laws.

ὀδόντας καθάπερ θῆρες ἔβρυχον, ἔτι ῥητορεύοντα τὸν Στέφανον καταπιεῖν

ὀδόντες αὐτῶν ὅπλα καὶ βέλη, καὶ ἡ γλῶσσα αὐτῶν μάχαιρα ὀξεῖα.» Στέφανος δὲ οὐ
πρὸς αὐτούς, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν τοὺς ὀφθαλ μοὺς εἶχεν, καὶ τῆς γῆς ἀφέμενος εἰς
τὰς αὐλὰς τῶν οὐρανῶν ἠπείγετο, καὶ λαμπρᾷ τῇ φωνῇ «Ἰδοὺ θεωρῶ τοὺς οὐρανοὺς

τοῖς εἰσελθεῖν βουλομένοις ἀνέῳ κται. Ὁ ἀνδρεῖος συντόνως ἀθλείτω· ὁ γνήσιος
ὁπλίτης νῦν χρη σάσθω τοῖς ὅπλοις, νῦν ἐνδειξάσθω τῆς ῥώμης τὸ μέγεθος. Ὁ γὰρ
ἀγωνοθέτης ἐφορᾷ· τοὺς στεφάνους καὶ τὰ βραβεῖα διανέμων ἐφέστηκεν.
24 «Ἰδοὺ θεωρῶ τοὺς οὐρανοὺς ἀνεῳγότας.» Καὶ τίς ὁ ἀνοίξας, οὐκ ἀφῆκεν
ἀγνοεῖν τὸν εἰδέναι βουλόμενον. Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο κέκραγεν· «Καὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ
ἀνθρώπου ἑστῶτα ἐκ δε ξιῶν τοῦ θεοῦ», τὸν θεὸν Λόγον τὸν σαρκωθέντα λέγων.
Ἀφ' οὗ γὰρ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου γεγένηται, ἀφ' οὗ ὁ ἐκ Πα τρὸς αὐτὸς ἐκ
παρθένου ἐνέστη τῇ γῇ καὶ τοῖς οὐρανοῖς ὅριον, περιῄρηται τῆς ἔχθρας τὸ
μεσότοιχον, ἐκποδὼν ὁ φραγμός, κοινὰ τοῖς ἀγγέλοις καὶ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις τὰ τῆς
πολιτείας, ἐὰν οἱ ἄνθρωποι βούλωνται. Ἔξεστιν ἐπὶ γῆς οὖσιν ἐν οὐρανῷ στρατεύε
σθαι, κάτω τῇ σαρκὶ τυγχάνειν, ἄνω παρεῖναι τῷ πνεύματι, εἶναι μετὰ τοῦ πηλοῦ τῷ
πηλῷ, μετὰ δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ τῷ νῷ.
25 Ταῦτα μὲν οὖν ἐθεολόγει Στέφανος· βοαὶ δὲ τὴν ἐν τά ξει θεολογίαν
ἄτακτοι, καὶ βοαὶ τὰς βοὰς διεδέχοντο· καὶ σφενδόναι λίθων τοῖς τῶν ἱερῶν νόμων

review_notes: The section opens mid-sentence, closing the words of the Jews begun in the previous section.
τοὺς στρατιώτας <ὡς> νεκρούς: the editor's supplement 'like' is followed, so 'the soldiers like dead men' (Matthew 28:4).
Acts 7:51: Hesychius reads σκληροκάρδιοι, 'hard-hearted', where the usual text of Acts has σκληροτράχηλοι, 'stiff-necked'; the English follows Hesychius.
The last sentence ('and stones from slings followed the teachings of the holy laws') runs across into the next section in the Greek; it is translated whole here.
